newsitem.title: CANADA: MOTOR RACING-MECHANICAL FAILURE LIKELY CAUSE OF PANIS CRASH.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-MECHANICAL FAILURE LIKELY CAUSE OF PANIS CRASH.

text.p: Mechanical failure, probably in the rear suspension, has been blamed for the serious accident to Frenchman Oliver Panis which cut short Sunday's Canadian Grand Prix.

Panis suffered double fractures of both legs when his Mugen-Honda powered car slid out of control on the 51st of 69 scheduled laps. The race, already marred by a series of accidents, was red-flagged to a halt three laps later and awarded to Germany's twice world champion Michael Schumacher.
Team boss Alain Prost said Panis's car had been hit from behind at the start of the race.

"Then he radioed to say he hit a rail during his in-lap prior to his third pit stop afer 43 laps," Prost said. "It appears obvious that one or the other of these incidents caused the failure of a mechanical component at the rear of his car."

As the majority of the Formula One circus hurriedly packed their bags for an overnight return to Europe, Prost was busy making plans to fly his 30-year-old driver back to Paris later this week by air ambulance.
He left several members of his team behind in Montreal to visit Panis at the city's Sacre Coeur Hospital and help look after him after the operation on his legs.

Rival team boss Tom Walkinshaw of Arrows offered Prost the use of his private plane to fly Panis home but his offer was declined because of the need to give the Frenchman full medical attention on board the flight.

While the explanation for Panis' crash was welcomed by many paddock observers, it did not altogether quell the alarm felt at seeing the race effectively abandoned because of the number, and severity, of the accidents.
Many were caused by the slippery nature of the track in the hot conditions which could partly be explained by the high tyre wear experienced by all the teams.

Tyre wear has become a problem this year and may be explained by the escalation of the 'tyre war' between Goodyear and Bridgestone which has encouraged the use of softer compounds in search of faster lap times.

Schumacher, whose second victory of the season for the Ferrai team and the 24th of his career lifted him back on top of the drivers' championship, said: "Tyre problems dominated the race. On my first set, I did not push too hard to look after them and I was helped by the arrival of the Safety Car.

"But after (Jacques) Villeneuve retired I had to push hard to keep ahead of (Giancarlo) Fisichella. We had planned to make two stops, but my third set were so badly damaged that I had to make an extra stop."
Jacques Villeneuve, the Canadian who was favourite to win the race, crashed out on the second lap in his Williams and was one of the 12 non-finishers in the field of 22.

Villeneuve, now seven points behind Schumacher in the drivers' title race after seven of the season's scheduled 17 races, said: "I made a mistake. It was a beginner's mistake, I guess, so it is very annoying.

"The car was very strong because at that point I wasn't even pushing. I was just following Michael from far away as he was eating up his tyres. I was taking it easy, not pushing, aiming to look after mine.
"It was amazing how slippery it was. It surprised me. This is going to be a hard one to swallow. There is no point to stop eating or lose sleep over it, but it's going to be difficult to accept."
Villeneuve will return to work with Williams in testing at Magny-Cours in France later this week in a bid to recharge his bid for the title at the French Grand Prix in 13 days' time.
But Schumacher and Ferrari anticipate improvements to their cars over the next month and a close scrap for the championship is in prospect. REUTER
